5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency, the disease caused by germline *ALDH5A1* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ssadh_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *ALDH5A1* variant or a diagnosis of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *ALDH5A1* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task

63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```

80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:

82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```

86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.

97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.

104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *ALDH5A1* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.

115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.

The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".

1	PMID: 27896081
2	PMCID: PMC5121295
3	DOI: 10.1016/j.ymgmr.2014.02.005
4	Title: Evidence of redox imbalance in a patient with succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
5	Journal: Molecular Genetics and Metabolism Reports (2014)
6	Authors: Niemi Anna-Kaisa; Brown Candida; Moore Tereza; Enns Gregory M; Cowan Tina M
7	
8	# Evidence of redox imbalance in a patient with succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractThe pathophysiology of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is not completely understood. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial pathology, and low reduced glutathione levels have been demonstrated in mice, but no studies have been reported in humans. We report on a patient with SSADH deficiency in whom we found low levels of blood reduced glutathione (GSH), and elevations of dicarboxylic acids in urine, suggestive of possible redox imbalance and/or mitochondrial dysfunction. Thus, targeting the oxidative stress axis may be a potential therapeutic approach if our findings are confirmed in other patients.Keywords: SSADH, Oxidative stress, Glutathione, GSH, Mitochondria
13	
14	## Introduction
15	
16	1.
17	
18	Succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH; EC 1.2.1.24) deficiency is a rare disorder (OMIM 271980) of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) degradation caused by mutations in ALDH5A1[1], [2]. In this disorder, succinic semialdehyde, the transamination product of GABA, is not converted to succinic acid but instead into 4-hydroxybutyric acid (γ-hydroxybutyric acid, GHB) and other related metabolites including 4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acids [3]. The diagnosis of SSADH deficiency is based on detecting elevated levels of 4-hydroxybutyric and related metabolites in body fluids including urine [3], [4]. The clinical picture of SSADH deficiency is variable, with the most common manifestations being intellectual disability, expressive language deficits, epilepsy, hypotonia, ataxia, sleep disorders, and psychiatric disturbances [1], [5], [6]. Therapeutic interventions attempted in humans or murine models have included vigabatrin [7], phenobarbital [8], and taurine [9], but no treatment has shown consistent significant efficacy. Thus, novel therapeutic approaches are needed.
19	
20	The pathophysiology of SSADH deficiency is not completely understood. It is unclear whether elevated GABA, GHB, or a secondary deficiency of tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, or Krebs cycle, intermediates due to lack of conversion of succinic semialdehyde to succinic acid, or some another mechanism contributes to the clinical phenotype of these patients. Mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress have been suggested to play a role by both in vitro and murine model studies [10], [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]. Decreased total radical-trapping potential (TRAP), increased lipid peroxidation and altered antioxidant enzyme activities have been demonstrated in SSADH deficient mice [10], [13], [14], [15], [17]. In addition, patients with SSADH deficiency typically have increased levels of urinary dicarboxylic acids that can sometimes be seen in the presence of mitochondrial dysfunction [2], [3].
21	
22	Glutathione (GSH) is the most abundant low-molecular-weight thiol, and effectively scavenges free radicals and other reactive oxygen species directly and indirectly through enzymatic reactions. Decreased GSH levels are used as a marker of oxidative stress [18], [19], [20] and have been demonstrated in the liver [14] and in the cerebral cortex of SSADH deficient mice [10], [14], [16]. To date, no such studies have been reported in humans.
23	
24	To evaluate whether signs of oxidative stress suggested by murine models can be demonstrated in humans, we measured blood glutathione levels longitudinally in a 10-month old patient with SSADH deficiency.
25	
26	## Patient report and results
27	
28	2.
29	
30	The patient was born after an uncomplicated pregnancy to non-consanguineous parents via cesarean section due to prolonged labor. Her birth parameters were normal. At 1.5 months of age, she developed stiffening episodes characterized by appearance of holding her breath, appearing startled, and arm extension. On examination at 1.5 months of age she had hypotonia, head lag, a stiffening episode lasting for seconds, some downward inner movement of the eyes at that point, and an exaggerated Moro reflex and startle response. This exaggerated Moro response was not present anymore at age 4 months. At age 4 months the patient was not able to maintain head control against gravity, but was able to lift her extremities. Deep tendon reflexes were preserved at first evaluation at 1.5 months of age but hyporeflexia was present thereafter.
31	
32	Brain MRI at age 4 months was normal and has not been repeated. Electroencephalogram (EEG) at age showed waking background composed predominantly of alpha, theta and delta range activity with appropriate anterior to posterior gradient which was lost asleep with the development of high amplitude delta activity with frequent bursts of sharpened alpha/beta range activity highest in amplitude on the fronto/central electrodes. Ophthalmological evaluation was repeatedly normal. Plasma amino acids, plasma total and free carnitine, plasma acylcarnitine profile, creatine kinase, electrolytes, complete blood count, lactate, and thyroid function tests were normal. Urine organic acids showed a marked elevation of 4-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB) as well as abnormal elevations of 4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acid lactones, glycolic, 3-hydroxypropionic, glutaric, adipic, and 2-hydroxyglutaric acids consistent with the diagnosis of SSADH deficiency. Sequencing of ALDH5A1 revealed a heterozygous splice site variant c.610-612A>G (IVS3-2A>G) in intron 3, and a heterozygous missense mutation c.1333A>C (p.M445L) in exon 9. Both mutations have been previously reported [8], [21] and are considered pathogenic. Biparental inheritance was confirmed.
33	
34	The patient was started on vigabatrin (up to 150 mg/kg/d) and taurine (160 mg/kg/d) at 5 months of age. At age 7–8 months she was able to roll over, grab objects, push up to support herself on her arms, hold her head up briefly, and made babbling sounds. On physical examination she continued to have severe diffuse though head lag had improved and an exaggerated startle response was not present.
35	
36	We measured whole blood GSH levels in our patient by liquid-chromatography tandem mass spectrometry [22]. The GSH level in our patient was 585 μM at age 5 months, 702 μM at age 9 months, and 698 μM at age 10 months (controls: 900 μM ± 140, n = 59). The mean value of all three determinations (662 μM) was significantly different from controls in an unpaired T-test (p = 0.011).
37	
38	## Discussion
39	
40	3.
41	
42	We report a patient with an early-onset SSADH deficiency with low GSH levels in blood suggesting increased oxidative stress. This is consistent with reduced levels of GSH reported in the liver and brain of mice with SSADH deficiency [10], [14], [16]. Our observation further supports the hypothesis of oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in SSADH deficiency suggested by in vitro studies and experimental models [10], [11], [12], [14], [15], [16]. Administration of GHB, which accumulates in SSADH deficiency, has been demonstrated to induce oxidative stress in the cerebral cortex of rats by increasing lipid peroxidation [16]. Succinic semialdehyde (SSA), the substrate of SSADH enzyme, is a reactive carbonyl and may lead to oxidative stress [13], [23]. Furthermore, SSADH enzyme is also responsible for metabolism of the lipid peroxidation aldehyde 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal (4-HNE), an intermediate known to induce oxidant stress [14], [23]. Decreased activities of mitochondrial complexes I–IV have also been reported in hippocampus of a murine model of SSADH deficiency [16].
43	
44	Low glutathione levels have been demonstrated in the blood of patients with primary mitochondrial disease [24] as well as in the blood and liver tissue of patients with organic acidemias such as methylmalonic acidemia [24], [25], [26] indicating secondary mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance organic acidemias. Increased lipid peroxidation [14], [15], [23] and low glutathione levels [10], [14], [16] in murine models of SSADH deficiency as well as dicarboxylic aciduria reported in patients [3] and mitochondrial dysfunction in SSADH deficiency, similar to other organic acidemias.
45	
46	We report on a patient with early-onset SSADH deficiency for which we demonstrate persistently low GSH levels and abnormal elevations of some dicarboxylic acids in urine suggesting possible redox imbalance and/or mitochondrial dysfunction. This is the first such report on human SSADH and consistent with studies from murine models. Targeting the oxidative stress axis, e.g. by supplementing with N-acetylcysteine or other antioxidants, may be a viable treatment modality for SSADH deficiency and other organic acidemias if our initial findings are confirmed in other patients.

messages.content: 24	To evaluate whether signs of oxidative stress suggested by murine models can be demonstrated in humans, we measured blood glutathione levels longitudinally in a 10-month old patient with SSADH deficiency.

32	Brain MRI at age 4 months was normal and has not been repeated. Electroencephalogram (EEG) at age showed waking background composed predominantly of alpha, theta and delta range activity with appropriate anterior to posterior gradient which was lost asleep with the development of high amplitude delta activity with frequent bursts of sharpened alpha/beta range activity highest in amplitude on the fronto/central electrodes. Ophthalmological evaluation was repeatedly normal. Plasma amino acids, plasma total and free carnitine, plasma acylcarnitine profile, creatine kinase, electrolytes, complete blood count, lactate, and thyroid function tests were normal. Urine organic acids showed a marked elevation of 4-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB) as well as abnormal elevations of 4,5-dihydroxyhexanoic acid lactones, glycolic, 3-hydroxypropionic, glutaric, adipic, and 2-hydroxyglutaric acids consistent with the diagnosis of SSADH deficiency. Sequencing of ALDH5A1 revealed a heterozygous splice site variant c.610-612A>G (IVS3-2A>G) in intron 3, and a heterozygous missense mutation c.1333A>C (p.M445L) in exon 9. Both mutations have been previously reported [8], [21] and are considered pathogenic. Biparental inheritance was confirmed.

34	The patient was started on vigabatrin (up to 150 mg/kg/d) and taurine (160 mg/kg/d) at 5 months of age. At age 7–8 months she was able to roll over, grab objects, push up to support herself on her arms, hold her head up briefly, and made babbling sounds. On physical examination she continued to have severe diffuse though head lag had improved and an exaggerated startle response was not present.

At age 7–8 months she was able to roll over, grab objects, push up to support herself on her arms, hold her head up briefly, and made babbling sounds. 36	We measured whole blood GSH levels in our patient by liquid-chromatography tandem mass spectrometry [22]. The GSH level in our patient was 585 μM at age 5 months, 702 μM at age 9 months, and 698 μM at age 10 months (controls: 900 μM ± 140, n = 59). The mean value of all three determinations (662 μM) was significantly different from controls in an unpaired T-test (p = 0.011).

12	AbstractThe pathophysiology of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency is not completely understood. Oxidative stress, mitochondrial pathology, and low reduced glutathione levels have been demonstrated in mice, but no studies have been reported in humans. We report on a patient with SSADH deficiency in whom we found low levels of blood reduced glutathione (GSH), and elevations of dicarboxylic acids in urine, suggestive of possible redox imbalance and/or mitochondrial dysfunction. Thus, targeting the oxidative stress axis may be a potential therapeutic approach if our findings are confirmed in other patients.Keywords: SSADH, Oxidative stress, Glutathione, GSH, Mitochondria
